items.text: Rest addresses depletion. It doesn't reduce the demands that caused it. You can't rest your way out of burnout while the structural load stays the same.
items.rationale: Plainspoken reframe that names the core distinction — rest vs. demand reduction — without clinical language. Validates the burnout survivor's experience that 'just rest more' keeps failing them.

items.text: If rest alone could fix autistic burnout, a good holiday would do it. What's actually changed when burnout finally lifts — and what had to give?
items.rationale: Opens a genuine community conversation about what demand reduction looks like in practice. The holiday framing is concrete and instantly recognisable to burnout survivors without making any claims.

items.text: Demand avoidance in adults isn't laziness or attitude. It's a nervous system firing a genuine threat signal. Can't, not won't. That difference matters.
items.rationale: Delivers the 'can't not won't' reframe in its most direct form. Uses community-validated framing from the May 2026 PDA discourse without overstating mechanism as medical fact.

items.text: A lot of late-diagnosed people expect relief and get grief instead. Grief for every year you didn't have a name for it. That's not ingratitude. It's what happens when a system fails you early.
items.rationale: Names the post-diagnosis grief experience precisely and places the failure on the system, not the person. No advice, no silver lining — pure validation of an under-named experience.

items.text: The ADHD part craves novelty. The autistic part needs sameness. That's not a personality quirk — it's two nervous-system drives in direct opposition, every single day.
items.rationale: The most compressed version of the AuDHD internal-conflict framing. 'Every single day' lands the exhaustion without elaboration. Drawn directly from the NatGeo and Substack framing in the briefing.

items.text: AuDHD isn't just 'both at once.' It's ADHD pulling toward novelty while autism braces for change — a conflict that runs in the background every waking hour and drains energy outsiders can't see.
items.rationale: Builds on the validation angle with a more specific mechanical description. 'Outsiders can't see' names the invisibility of the burden, a key source of non-recognition for AuDHD people.

items.text: Interoception works differently in many autistic people — hunger, pain, fatigue often don't signal clearly until they tip over. The burnout wasn't sudden. The warning system just didn't deliver on time.
items.rationale: Introduces the interoception mechanism concretely without jargon overload. 'Didn't deliver on time' frames it as a data failure, not a personal failure, without requiring the reader to understand neuroscience.

items.text: The story is 'you should have noticed sooner.' But if your interoceptive signals aren't arriving clearly, you weren't ignoring your body. Your body wasn't giving you reliable data.
items.rationale: Reframes the 'should have known better' self-blame as a data-delivery failure, not a character failure. Works standalone and pairs naturally with the post above without being a thread.

items.text: Low-demand parenting means reducing unnecessary demands, not all of them. Predictability, routines, collaborative choice — those aren't optional extras. They're what actually keeps the nervous system calmer.
items.rationale: Gives PDA parents the precise distinction they need without being prescriptive or preachy. Addresses the live debate around misapplication of low-demand approaches by naming what the approach actually requires.

items.text: 81% of neurodivergent employees mask at work — and burnout risk is three times higher for those who do. Masking isn't a soft concern. It's an occupational hazard that just hasn't been named as one yet.
items.rationale: Pairs the concrete stat with structural framing ('occupational hazard') to shift masking from a personal-resilience conversation to a systems one. The final sentence is the sharpest part.
items.sensitivity_flag: The 81% and 3x burnout figures appear in secondary 2026 coverage; verify the primary research source before posting to ensure the specific numbers are accurate.

items.text: If 81% of neurodivergent employees are masking at work, what would it actually take to make one fewer mask necessary?
items.rationale: Tight question that redirects the masking conversation from individual coping to structural accountability. Short format increases shareability and invites genuine responses without baiting outrage.
items.sensitivity_flag: The 81% figure is drawn from secondary coverage; verify the primary research source before posting.

items.text: For many PDAers, the 'just do it for yourself, nobody's watching' advice still doesn't work. The freeze hits your own to-do list just as hard. A demand is a demand even when you wrote it.
items.rationale: Names a highly specific and isolating PDA experience that almost no mainstream content addresses. 'A demand is a demand even when you wrote it' is the quotable line. No fix offered — just the naming.
